Country in [[South Asia]] (pop., 2023: over 241.5 million), officially the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, a federal parliamentary republic of 796,095 sq km. It is the fifth-most populous country, with the second-largest Muslim population in the world. [[Islamabad]] is the capital and [[Karachi]] the largest city and financial center. Pakistan borders the Arabian Sea on the south and shares land borders with [[India]] to the east, Afghanistan to the west, Iran to the southwest, and China to the northeast.

The area is the site of the 8,500-year-old Neolithic site of Mehrgarh, the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] of the Bronze Age, and the Gandhara civilization. It was later ruled by the Achaemenid, Maurya, Kushan, Gupta, Ghaznavid, and Mughal empires and dynasties, among others, and finally by the [[British Raj]] from 1858 to 1947.

Pakistan became independent in 1947 through the [[Partition of India]], which awarded separate statehood to British India's Muslim-majority regions and was accompanied by mass migration and loss of life. It adopted a republican constitution in 1956 and became an Islamic republic with two separate provinces, East and West Pakistan. East Pakistan seceded as [[Bangladesh]] in 1971 after a nine-month civil war. Governments since have alternated between civilian and military, democratic and authoritarian. Islam is the state religion, and over 96% of the population is Muslim.

Pakistan is a declared nuclear-weapon state with the world's seventh-largest standing armed forces. Its economy is ranked among the world's emerging and growth-leading economies, but the country faces poverty, illiteracy, corruption, and terrorism. It belongs to the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations, and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

Scientific study of the life of the past, mainly but not exclusively through [[Fossil|fossils]]. Paleontologists use fossils to classify organisms, measure geologic time, and assess the interactions between prehistoric organisms and their environment. Paleontological observations are known from at least the 6th century BC, but the science's foundation dates to the work of [[Georges Cuvier]] in 1796, who demonstrated evidence for [[Extinction|extinction]] and showed that the life of the past was not necessarily the same as that of the present. The French word *paléontologie* was introduced in 1822. [[Charles Darwin]] later popularized the concept of [[Evolution|evolution]]; evolution and extinction are understood as complementary processes that shaped the history of life.

The field overlaps most with [[Geology|geology]] and [[Biology|biology]], and also with ecology, chemistry, physics, and mathematics. Invertebrate paleontology has traditionally been tied to geology and biostratigraphy, areas with both commercial and academic drivers, while vertebrate paleontology has been closer to biology. Fieldwork, laboratory preparation, and comparative anatomy remain core components. Other subfields include micropaleontology, paleobotany, paleobiology, and paleoecology. Methods include stratigraphy, radiometric dating, and cladistics, and biostratigraphy is used to reconstruct the geologic time scale. Theoretical analysis introduced in the 1950s and 1960s led to more focused fields studying changing geography and climate, phylogenetic relationships, and how fossilization occurs and what biases affect the fossil record.

Paleontology draws attention in mass media comparable to that given to astrophysics and global health. Public interest can be traced to the mythologies of indigenous peoples and to the interpretation of fossils as the bones of dragons or giants. Prehistoric life inspires toys, television, film, computer games, and tourism, with budgets that often exceed funding within the field itself.

Thin sheet of matted [[Cellulose|cellulose]] fibers, largely derived from lignocellulose, made from a pulp dissolved into a slurry that is drained and dried into sheets. The word derives from Latin *papyrus*, but [[Papyrus|papyrus]], a lamination of natural plant fiber, is a separate technology from paper, which is made from fibers changed by maceration.

Papermaking developed in [[East Asia]] at least as early as AD 105 by the Han court eunuch [[Cai Lun]], although paper-like material from the 2nd century BC has been found in [[China]]. Papyrus was replaced because it was limited geographically to Egypt, more expensive and laborious to produce, and more fragile. Popular history credits the Battle of Talas in 751 with spreading papermaking to the Islamic world, but an archive of 76 paper writings found in Panjikent predates the city's capture by Arabs in 722, and paper was being made in [[Baghdad]] by the late 8th century. Knowledge of paper spread to Europe in the 13th century, where the first water-powered paper mills were built.

Before industrialization the most common paper was rag paper. In the 19th century, industrialization greatly reduced costs; Charles Fenerty of Canada and Friedrich Gottlob Keller of Germany independently developed processes for pulping wood fibers, and with the [[Second Industrial Revolution]] pulpwood paper became dominant. Chemical pulping dissolves lignin; the kraft process, invented in the 1870s, is now the most common and recovers and reuses all inorganic reagents. Mechanical pulping yields more than 95%, but the remaining lignin turns paper yellow and brittle over time. Packaging accounts for about 65% of output, and manufacture contributes to [[Deforestation|deforestation]] if forests are unmanaged.

Process of promoting and supporting a child's physical, cognitive, social, emotional, and educational development from infancy to adulthood. Parenting concerns the raising of a child and is not exclusively a biological relationship. The most common caregivers are biological [[Parent|parents]], but a caregiver may be an older sibling, step-parent, [[Grandparent|grandparent]], legal guardian, aunt, uncle, other relative, or family friend. [[Government|Governments]] and society may also have a role. Orphaned or abandoned children may be cared for by non-relatives, adopted, raised in foster care, or placed in an [[Orphanage|orphanage]].

Styles vary by historical period, [[Culture|culture]], [[Social class|social class]], and personal preferences, and no single style is necessarily correct, since styles affect children differently depending on circumstances and temperament. Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind proposed three main styles, authoritative, authoritarian, and permissive, later expanded to four with an uninvolved style. Authoritative parenting, which Baumrind called the "just right" style, combines medium demands with medium responsiveness and relies on positive reinforcement and infrequent punishment; children raised this way score higher in competence, mental health, and social development. Authoritarian parenting is rigid and strict, with high demands, little responsiveness, and non-negotiable rules; it is strongly associated with corporal punishment, and in 1983 Baumrind found that such children were less cheerful, moodier, and more vulnerable to stress. Permissive parenting (undemanding, with little punishment) has been more popular among middle-class than working-class families roughly since the end of World War II. Critics regard Baumrind's typology as overly broad and as idealizing the authoritative style.

Research also indicates that parents' own attachment history and psychopathology can influence parental sensitivity and child outcomes, and that warm adoptive parenting is associated with reduced behavioral problems in adopted children over time.

Capital and largest city of [[France]] (city pop., 2.04 million; metropolitan area, 2023: 13.3 million), on the Seine in the center of the [[Île-de-France]] region. Paris covers 105.4 sq km and is the largest metropolitan area and fourth-most populous city in the [[European Union]]. It is nicknamed the "City of Light" mainly for its leading role in the [[Age of Enlightenment]]; some accounts also cite the installation of street lamps under Louis XIV in the mid-17th century. Haussmann's renovation gave rise to the modern city known as the "capital of the 19th century."

The ancient settlement was first mentioned in the mid-1st century BC by [[Julius Caesar]] as Lutetia Parisiorum, "Lutetia of the Parisii," after the Gallic tribe that had inhabited the area since about the middle of the 3rd century BC. Caesar conquered the Paris Basin in 52 BC. Clovis the Frank made the city his capital from 508. After the 987 election of Hugh Capet, Count of Paris, as king, it gradually became the largest and most prosperous city in France.

The president of France and both houses of Parliament sit in Paris, which hosts organizations including [[UNESCO]], the OECD, and the European Space Agency. It is a major railway, motorway, and air-transport hub. The [[Louvre]] is the largest and most-visited museum in the world, and the Eiffel Tower is among its landmarks. Parts of the city along the Seine have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The Île-de-France region contributes about 30% of France's GDP. Paris hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924, and 2024.

Branch of physics, also called high-energy physics, that studies the fundamental particles and forces that constitute matter and radiation. The [[Standard Model]], the dominant theory, classifies fundamental particles as fermions (matter particles) and bosons (force-carrying particles). Ordinary matter is made only from the first of three fermion generations: up and down [[Quark|quarks]], which form protons and neutrons, and electrons and electron neutrinos. Quarks cannot exist alone but form hadrons; baryons contain an odd number of quarks and mesons an even number. Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite electric charge, such as the positron for the electron, and such particles could form [[Antimatter|antimatter]].

The idea that matter is composed of elementary particles dates from at least the 6th century BC. Nuclear fission was proved in 1939 by [[Lise Meitner]], based on experiments by Otto Hahn, and nuclear fusion by [[Hans Bethe]] the same year. In the 1950s and 1960s collisions at ever higher energies revealed a bewildering "particle zoo," which the Standard Model, formulated in the 1970s, explained as combinations of a small number of more fundamental particles. The model contains 24 fundamental fermions, eight gluons, the W⁻, W⁺, and Z bosons, and the photon. It also predicted the [[Higgs boson]]; on July 4, 2012, physicists at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] at [[CERN]] announced a new particle that behaves as expected for it.

The Standard Model agrees with almost all experimental tests, but most particle physicists consider it incomplete. It does not incorporate gravity, and measurements of neutrino mass provide the first experimental deviations from it.

State of harmony in the absence of hostility and violence. In a societal sense, the term commonly means a lack of conflict and freedom from fear of violence between individuals or groups. Promotion of peace is a core tenet of many philosophies, religions, and ideologies, including [[Buddhism]], [[Christianity]], Jainism, and [[Islam]]; of figures such as [[Mahatma Gandhi]] and [[Martin Luther King Jr.]]; of writings such as [[Immanuel Kant]]'s *Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch*; and of pacifism. No universal definition exists; the meaning of peace and its symbols varies with culture, context, and history.

The English word comes from Anglo-French *pes* and Old French *pais*, from Latin *pax*. From c. 1300 it was used in greetings as a translation of the Hebrew *shalom*.

Peace has been forged through diplomacy, as in royal marriages between Greek princesses and the kings of Phrygia and Lydia around 800 BC and 600 BC. It has also been enforced by victors through violence and coercion. In *Agricola*, [[Tacitus]] attributes to the Caledonian chieftain Calgacus the charge that the Romans, "where they make a desert, they call it peace." Societal peace can be understood as the simple absence of war, or as absence of war accompanied by justice, mutual respect, respect for law, and good will. Scholars likewise distinguish negative peace, the mere cessation of direct violence, from positive peace, which includes equitable institutions and social justice. Debate continues over whether pacifist ideals suffice or whether military readiness and balances of power better secure stability, and the democratic peace theory faces scrutiny over its causal claims. Since 1945 the [[United Nations]] and its Security Council have operated under the aim of resolving conflicts without war, though nations have entered numerous military conflicts since.

Identification, interpretation, and organization of sensory information in order to represent and understand the environment. The term comes from Latin *perceptio* ('gathering, receiving'). All perception involves signals passing through the [[Nervous system|nervous system]], resulting from physical or chemical stimulation of the sensory system: vision involves light striking the retina, smell is mediated by odor molecules, and hearing involves pressure waves. It is not passive receipt of these signals but is shaped by the perceiver's [[Learning|learning]], [[Memory|memory]], expectation, and [[Attention|attention]].

The process begins with a distal stimulus, an object in the real world, which stimulates the sensory organs. These transform the input energy into neural activity, called transduction, and the raw pattern is the proximal stimulus. Once transmitted to the [[Brain|brain]] and processed, it yields the percept, the mental re-creation of the distal stimulus.

Perception depends on complex nervous system functions but seems effortless because the processing happens outside conscious awareness. Since the rise of experimental [[Psychology|psychology]] in the 19th century, understanding has advanced through psychophysics, sensory neuroscience, and computational study. Illusions and ambiguous images show that perceptual systems actively and pre-consciously try to make sense of their input. Debate continues over whether perception is an active process of hypothesis testing, analogous to science, or whether sensory information is rich enough to make this unnecessary. Brains are modular, with different areas processing different kinds of sensory information, often in sensory maps, and the modules influence each other; taste, for instance, is strongly influenced by smell. Philosophers ask to what extent qualities such as sound, smell, or color exist in objective reality rather than in the mind of the perceiver.

Arts such as [[Music|music]], [[Dance|dance]], and drama performed for an audience, distinguished from the visual arts, which produce physical or static objects. They are performed in purpose-built buildings such as theaters and opera houses, in open-air festivals and street settings, and in recorded formats such as film and television. Traditions exist in every society. Music and dance date to prehistoric times, while theatrical forms appear in [[Ancient Greece]], India, and China, serving combinations of religious, ceremonial, and entertainment functions. Japanese [[Noh]] and [[Kabuki]] and Indian classical dance have been recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Theater acts out stories before an audience through speech, gesture, music, dance, and spectacle, and is linked to ritual in ancient cultures. Its most familiar form is the scripted play; it has also diversified into musicals, which integrate song and dance, and [[Opera|opera]], in which all the words are set to music. In improvisational theater actors invent material instead of following a script. Dance is human movement, typically rhythmic and to music, ranging from functional forms such as folk dance to codified techniques such as ballet; choreography is the art of composing dances. Modern dance emerged in the 20th century as a response to the strictures of ballet. Music organizes sound using timbre, pitch, rhythm, and dynamics and is divided into genres such as folk, jazz, hip-hop, pop, and rock. Opera originated in Italy at the end of the 16th century and became the prestige entertainment of aristocratic and later bourgeois society. The field also includes magic, mime, spoken word, puppetry, performance art, and stand-up comedy.

As early as the 19th century BC, a large religious ceremony in Egypt may have had theater-like elements; the Dramatic Ramesseum Papyrus has been interpreted as an early example of dramatic literature, although its classification remains debated. Greek playwrights including Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides developed tragedy in the 5th century BC, while Aristophanes, Cratinus, and Menander developed comedy. In India the *Natya Shastra*, a Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy attributed to Bharata and possibly compiled 200 BC–AD 200, formulated theatrical theory. In China the dramatic tradition goes back to the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC). Shadow puppetry emerged under the Han (202 BC–AD 220), Emperor Xuanzong established the Pear Garden to train performers under the Tang (618–907), and the Zaju variety play peaked under the Yuan (1271–1368), with Beijing opera as its descendant.

Western performing arts history spans Greek tragedy and comedy, medieval mystery plays, the emergence of opera and ballet in the Renaissance, and the Romantic expansion of grand opera. In the modernist revolutions of the early 20th century, [[Isadora Duncan]], [[Konstantin Stanislavski]], and Sergei Diaghilev reworked the principles of dance and theater. Audio and video recording has allowed private consumption of the performing arts.

Ordered arrangement of the [[Chemical element|chemical elements]] into rows ("periods") and columns ("groups"). Elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics, and the table is also divided into four roughly rectangular blocks. It depicts the periodic law, which states that when elements are arranged by their [[Atomic number|atomic numbers]], an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident.

The first generally accepted table was that of the Russian chemist [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] in 1869, who formulated the periodic law in terms of atomic mass. He left gaps for elements not yet known and successfully used the law to predict properties of some of them. The law was explained early in the 20th century by the discovery of atomic numbers and by pioneering work in [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. A recognizably modern form was reached in 1945 with Glenn T. Seaborg's discovery that the actinides are f-block rather than d-block elements.

Each element has a unique atomic number, the number of protons in its nucleus. Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are [[Isotope|isotopes]] of the same element and are grouped together in the table. A new row begins when a new electron shell receives its first electron, and columns are determined by [[Electron configuration|electron configuration]]; oxygen, sulfur, and selenium share a column because each has four electrons in the outermost p-subshell. Of the 118 known elements, the first 94 occur naturally, 83 of them primordial and 11 only in decay chains; the remaining 24, americium to oganesson (95–118), are [[Synthetic element|synthetic]]. By 2010 all 118 were known, completing the first seven rows.
